Instruments measure genuinely independent physical systems with measurement noise dominating; no causal coupling exists between labs and observational streams.

Systematic calibration drift or instrument hysteresis is present in individual instruments but proceeds slowly enough that day-10 baseline snapshot does not yet show clear nonlinearity; drift will emerge in post-baseline comparison (day 11+) or via day-1 vs. day-10 mean shift analysis.

Environmental coupling (temperature, vibration, magnetic field) is present but weak, filtered by instrument mechanical design, or phase-delayed between lab and observational streams such that simple Pearson correlation at fixed lags fails to detect it; multi-scale or nonlinear analysis required.

Measurement protocol introduces independent random noise (observer reflex jitter, instrument readout quantization, trial-to-trial handling variance) that dominates over any weak physical coupling; readings are valid but limited in sensitivity for detecting inter-instrument synchronization until sample sizes grow or noise sources are isolated.
Residual: an unidentified pattern in the data structure, timing of trials, or correlation analysis method that explains the widespread weak correlations despite physical expectations.

Transient mechanical disturbance or environmental shock on day 16 affecting pendulum_lab only; other instruments unaffected or buffered by different mechanical coupling; effect self-limiting and not indicative of drift.

Slow calibration drift in individual instruments is accumulating but remains below detection threshold at day 10 baseline cutoff; day-16 excursions in pendulum_lab reflect the tail of an emerging drift distribution, not yet flagged as level shift because sample size post-baseline (n=96 or subset) is insufficient to separate drift from noise.
Measurement protocol or operator change on day 16 (fatigue, procedure drift, equipment substitution) introduced a brief systematic bias or increased variance; physical instruments remain stable.

Instruments measure genuinely independent physical systems with measurement noise dominating; the day-16 pendulum_lab excursions are statistical flukes within the expected tail of the noise distribution, not evidence of coupling or drift.

Environmental coupling (temperature, vibration, magnetic field) is present and phase-delayed between instruments; weak correlations at fixed lags reflect this delay structure, and the day-16 anomaly may represent a transient environmental event affecting only mechanically sensitive instruments.
Residual: unidentified pattern in timing, trial sequencing, or data logging that creates spurious anomalies or masks real signals.

Instruments measure genuinely independent physical systems with measurement noise dominating; weak correlations are expected, and the 0.618 pendulum_lab–resonator_obs correlation is a statistical artifact of searching multiple lags and offsets (look-ahead bias).

Selective environmental coupling: instruments have different mechanical impedance or thermal time constants; a real but weak shared environmental driver (temperature, vibration, electromagnetic) produces inverted responses in pendulum vs. resonator systems, with phase lag of 3 days.

Calibration baseline set too early; true instrumental drift began post-day-10 and is now emerging, masked by trial-to-trial noise but visible in marginal statistics (z-scores 0.14–0.67) and the presence of outliers like day-16 excursions in pendulum_lab.

Data-collection protocol or instrument configuration changed between baseline (days 1–10) and post-baseline (days 11–26), altering the noise characteristics or bias structure without producing obvious level shifts; the weak correlations reflect this structural change rather than physical independence.
Residual: unidentified pattern in data structure, trial sequencing, event-ID clustering, or measurement metadata that creates spurious correlations or masks real signals.
